Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A gray tabby cat curled up asleep on a folded mustard knit blanket on a sunny windowsill

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

15 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: the cat's sleeping face, with its white muzzle and pink nose Light: soft daylight from the window on the leftHow this lesson was made

Tubes to get out

Get these out of the box before you start. Every paint in the lesson is mixed from them; squeeze out a little of each when its step comes up.

  • Titanium whitefirst in step 1
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Ultramarine bluefirst in step 1
  • Burnt siennafirst in step 4

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the blue-gray wallFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Blend the sky in the windowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Dab the shadowed leaves outsideRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Block in the folded blanketFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch filbert: Paint the white muzzle, chest, and pawsFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #4 round: Paint the pink ears and noseRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch angle: Paint the tabby stripesAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • small fan: Flick in the light furFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

All 15 paints and their recipes. Each step lists the ones it needs, so you can mix as you go

You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The yellow knit blanket; 2 The sleeping cat. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Dabbing, first in step 3.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 5.
  • Press and lift, first in step 9. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 12.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 14.
  • Flicking, first in step 15.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The wall and the view outside 4 steps

STEP 1 OF 15 · The wall and the view outside, 1 of 4

Blend the blue-gray wall

  1. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 13 in wide and 8 1/2 in tall.
  2. Paint a little past its left side, under where the white window frame and the yellow knit blanket will go.
  3. Paint: Soft blue-gray.
  4. Mix enough Soft blue-gray for this step and step 5; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  6. Start at the top of the wall with Soft blue-gray and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up more of it and paint the next band below. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  7. It should leave one smooth, even wall color, with soft joins where the bands meet.
  8. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  9. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from the window on the left, so keep every highlight in this painting on the window side. Paint the wall straight across where the window, blanket, and cat will go; they all go on top later. Colors dry a little darker, so test the mix on the palette edge first.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it here, adapted for this painting, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Adapted for this painting from the Side-to-side blend card, not checked yet

The general Side-to-side blend card (its file)

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start at the top of the wall and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up more Soft blue-gray and paint the band below. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. One smooth wall color, with a soft join where two wet bands meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend the wall side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two bands of the wall meet. Add a little more paint at the join and blend again.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.
The general Side-to-side blend card

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 15 · The wall and the view outside, 2 of 4

Blend the sky in the window

  1. Let the blue-gray wall dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paints, top to bottom: Pale sky blue, then Hazy blue-green.
  5. Mix enough Hazy blue-green for this step and step 3; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  7. Start with Pale sky blue at the top of the glass and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up Hazy blue-green and paint the lower part below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  8. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  9. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  10. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: Keep it to the narrow strip of glass on the left edge, as the Where picture shows: sky blue at the top, the green glow lower down. The leaves and frame go over it later.

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.

STEP 3 OF 15 · The wall and the view outside, 3 of 4

Dab the shadowed leaves outside

  1. Let the view through the window and the blue-gray wall dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 4 in tall.
  3. Paint: Hazy blue-green.
  4. Brush: #8 round. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.

Tip: These leaves are outside and far away, so keep them as soft dabs with no leaf shapes, in loose clumps with sky showing between.

Dabbing also called stippling

Adapted for this painting from the Dabbing card, not checked yet

The general Dabbing card (its file)

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap the leaves outside with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Soft dappled clumps of leaves that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap the sunlit green on the tops of the clumps, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Good for. foliage, with an old stiff brush, small dots, with the tip of a round

Tap the leaves, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of leafy dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A clump went too solid and hides the sky. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

STEP 4 OF 15 · The wall and the view outside, 4 of 4

Dab the sunlit leaves outside

  1. Let the leaves outside and the view through the window dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 4 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Sage leaf green.
  4. Brush: #8 round. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  5. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  6. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  7. Leave what step 3 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Tap the sunlit green mostly on the tops of the clumps, and leave the blue-green showing underneath and at the bottom of each clump.

The window frame 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 15 · The window frame, 1 of 2

Block in the window frame

  1. Let the wall and the view outside dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 4 1/2 in wide and 8 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the sleeping cat and the wooden sill will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the blue-gray wall, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  5. Paint: Soft blue-gray.
  6. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  7. Start with one simple shape: the upright post, a rectangle pulled straight down. Then add the rest in pieces on each side: the crossbar to the left and the ledge along the bottom.
  8. It should leave a frame made of distinct straight pieces with small gaps or overlaps where they meet.

Tip: Pull each bar in one straight stroke along its length: the upright post first, about 2 1/2 inches in from the left edge, then the crossbar near the top and the ledge sloping down. Then run one thin line along the back edge of the sill where it meets the wall, as the Where picture shows.

Light the white frame

  1. Let the white window frame, and the wall and the view outside dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

Stroke: Building from pieces, as in step 5.

The wooden sill 1 step

STEP 7 OF 15 · The wooden sill, 1 of 1

Blend the wood and the sun on the sill

  1. Let the window frame, and the wall and the view outside dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paints: Warm wood brown, then Sunny peach.
  4. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  5. Start with Warm wood brown, the darker color, stroking side to side across the sill. Without rinsing, lay two slanted bands of Sunny peach on the left end. Then stroke back over their edges several times.
  6. It should leave smooth brown wood with two soft peach bands of sun on the left, joined softly where the wet colors meet.
  7. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  8. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Keep the brush strokes long and level, running along the sill. The sun bands slant down to the left like the window's light; keep them soft at the edges.

The knit blanket 3 steps

STEP 8 OF 15 · The knit blanket, 1 of 3

Block in the folded blanket

  1. Let the wooden sill and the window frame dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 15 in wide and 5 in tall.
  4. Paint: Deep golden ochre.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  6. Start with one simple shape: a long rounded rectangle for the bottom roll. Then add the rest in curved pieces: the top roll above it, under where the cat will lie, and the rounded fold at the left end.
  7. It should leave the blanket as two long golden rolls with a soft line between them.

Tip: The blanket is two long rolls, one stacked on the other, with the top one tucked under where the cat will lie. Paint straight through under the cat.

STEP 9 OF 15 · The knit blanket, 2 of 3

Shade the gaps between the knit loops

  1. Let the yellow knit blanket and the wooden sill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.

Block in the curled-up cat

STEP 12 OF 15 · The cat's body, 2 of 2

Paint the white muzzle, chest, and paws

  1. Let the sleeping cat and the knit blanket dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 9 in wide and 6 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Soft fur white.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch filbert.
  5. Bend every stroke with the shape: from the top of each bump down along its curve, and around a round shape.
  6. It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
  7. Leave what step 11 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Soft fur white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The white is on the muzzle, a band down the chest, and the two front paws under the chin. Curve the strokes around the chest and paws, and pull the whiskers last with the brush tip, thin and outward from the muzzle.

Paint the tabby stripes

STEP 15 OF 15 · The cat's markings and fur, 3 of 3

Flick in the light fur

  1. Let the sleeping cat and the cat's body dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 15 in wide and 7 in tall.
  3. Paint: Light fur gray.
  4. Brush: small fan. Load: A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.
  5. A quick stroke out from the base along the way the fur lies, lifting off as it goes, so each mark thins at the tip.
  6. It should leave short tapered fur marks with broken tips, more of them on the lit side near the window.
  7. Leave what steps 11, 12, 13 and 14 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The fur turns into a flat, smooth patch, or the stripes lose their edges. Too much paint on the brush, or the flicks are blended together.
  9. Fix: wipe the brush nearly dry, make each flick short and separate, and let it dry before adding more.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Flick along the fur: outward from the face across the forehead and cheeks, and following the curve of the back and side. Put more flicks on the side near the window and leave the stripes' edges and the darker gray showing between them.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A gray tabby cat curled up asleep on a folded mustard-yellow knit blanket on a wooden sill, a window with green outside at the top left and a pale blue-gray wall behind.

Found in the image: just the picture (an AI-painted image, no bars, borders, or text)

Done: none

Why: Everything in the image is part of the scene to paint.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: extend

Left out: nothing; the first extend render brightened the wall to a saturated blue, so it was redone once with the colors held (kept the redo)

Why: No canvas was named, so fit-canvas picked 12x16, the standard size closest to the 3:2 photo; cropping it to 4:3 would cut the blanket or the cat's back, so the picture sits on the canvas and a render continued the wall and sill past the top and bottom.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things (the leaves outside the window are a few soft green shapes). No textures of hundreds of items: busy measured 0.0% fine texture; the knit is about a hundred chunky loops, which is one repeated mark built in passes, and the stripes are bold bands. No veined detail inside big shapes. About 7 parts, under the budget of 8 on a 192 sq in canvas.

Changed: none

Why: Every answer was no, so the lesson is made from the fitted photo.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.0% of the canvas

A cozy, calm picture: the sleeping tabby is the whole point, so the lesson spends most of its steps on the cat (shape, white patches, ears, stripes, fur) and keeps the room simple. The hard parts are the cat's curled shape, stripes that wrap around the body, and a knit blanket that has to read as knitted without painting every stitch.

Subject: A gray tabby cat curled up asleep on a folded mustard knit blanket on a sunny windowsill
Focal point: the cat's sleeping face, with its white muzzle and pink nose
Light: soft daylight from the window on the left

What it saw, back to front

  1. The blue-gray wall
  2. The view through the window
  3. The white window frame
  4. The wooden sill
  5. The yellow knit blanket
  6. The sleeping cat
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, is the only technique with version 2 keys and it fits: a plain wall and window behind, then the sill, the blanket, the cat, and the knit and fur texture in front, all built with simple repeated marks a beginner can make.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules), so pipeline v2 can't plan from it; and the owner picked paint-along for beginner acrylic lessons.

How the paint recipes were worked out15 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

    Mixer: 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow, a touch of red

  • Hazy blue-green Delta E 2.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow

  • Pale sky blue Delta E 6.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

  • Warm window white Delta E 1.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 8 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Warm wood brown Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

  • Sunny peach Delta E 1.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Mustard yellow Delta E 0.6

Why the steps go in this order15 steps

Back to front: the wall first, straight through behind everything; then the view through the glass and its leaves, the window frame over them, the sill, the blanket the cat lies on, and the cat last, from its flat shape through the white patches, the pink ears and nose, the stripes, and the fur flicks on top.

  1. 1. Blend the blue-gray wall

    The farthest thing and the biggest area, so it goes on first, straight through behind everything.

  2. 2. Blend the sky in the window

    The view outside is behind the frame, so its sky goes on before the leaves and bars.

  3. 3. Dab the shadowed leaves outside

    Foliage goes dark first, so the light taps have something to sit on.

  4. 4. Dab the sunlit leaves outside

    The sunlit taps go on top, leaving the dark showing.

  5. 5. Block in the window frame

    The frame sits over the view; its shadow color first, built from straight pieces.

  6. 6. Light the white frame

    The lit faces go over the dry shadow color, keeping the inner edges blue-gray.

  7. 7. Blend the wood and the sun on the sill

    The sill is behind the blanket, so the wood and the sun on it go on before the blanket.

  8. 8. Block in the folded blanket

    The blanket is under the cat, so it's painted before the cat, first as two flat rolls.

  9. 9. Shade the gaps between the knit loops

    The dark crease goes in before the light loops so the loops can sit next to it.

  10. 10. Light the knit loops

    The light loops make the knit; they go on last on the blanket, leaving gaps.

  11. 11. Block in the curled-up cat

    The subject, on top of everything behind it, starting as one flat shape.

  12. 12. Paint the white muzzle, chest, and paws

    The white patches go on the dry gray base before the markings, as the element says.

  13. 13. Paint the pink ears and nose

    The pink inside the ears and the nose are a marking of their own color.

  14. 14. Paint the tabby stripes

    The stripes go on the dry base after the pale patches, curving around the body.

  15. 15. Flick in the light fur

    Fur flicks go last, over the stripes' edges, to finish the painting.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

The background steps are flat fills, blends, and repeated dabs that the picture and words make clear. Three steps need a diagram: the cat appears whole in its block-in, the blanket is a shape of two stacked rolls, and the stripes have to follow the body's curve.

  • Step 8: Block in the folded blanket beginner check

    Noticed: The folded blanket is one golden shape, but it's really two rolls stacked, which the flat coat hides.

    Pieces: A long rounded rectangle for the bottom roll, a second one behind it on top, and the rounded fold at the left end.

  • Step 11: Block in the curled-up cat beginner check

    Noticed: The whole cat appears in one step as one gray shape; a beginner couldn't see where to start a curled-up animal.

    Pieces: The body as a big oval first, then the round head overlapping on its left, then two triangle ears, the way a teacher draws a sleeping cat.

  • Step 14: Paint the tabby stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The stripes' placement depends on the body's structure: they wrap around it, wide on the back and thin down the side, with short bands on the tail.

    Pieces: The body and head as done shapes, then four curved stripes from the back down the side, then short bands across the tail.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The window frame wouldn't work as an object: the background render kept it (it's part of the room), so it showed in every step before its own. As an area it came out clean, but no library element is for an area like that, so I drafted window-frame (issue #160).
  • The sun bands on the sill wouldn't outline: points and then hex colors both took scraps of the dark bars beside them. The sill carries them as a second paint in its blend.
  • check asked to merge Hazy sea green (window glass) and Blue-green leaf shadow because their recipes came out the same; the paints tool says never to merge by hand, so I merged them in plan.json as check said (one paint shared by window-view and leaves). The two rules disagree; the skill could say which wins.
  • The cut pictures carry colors no step paint names when an outline takes them: the deep blue shadow beside the window lands in the wall and frame-light steps, and two whiskers that cross the blanket appear in the blanket steps. Recorded as left.
  • The first canvas-extend render and the first finish both pushed the wall to a saturated blue; one redo each with 'keep the colors' fixed it.
  • No Agent tool in this session, so the text review was done in the same context (review_context: same).
